To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the binding of C9 to C5b-6 complexes at 0 or 32 degrees C does not result in bacterial killing but rather causes the formation of a C5b-91C91 complex.

the binding of C9 to C5b-71C81C91 complexes on the bacterial cell surface at low temperature is insufficient to kill the bacteria, but at 32 to 37 degrees C, binding of C9 leads to rapid formation of transmural pores and bacterial cell lysis.

(i) C9 binds to the outer membrane in a temperature-dependent manner; (ii) C5b-91C9 complexes are not lethal to E. coli; (iii) C5b-C91C9 complexes cause rapid disruption of the outer and inner membrane permeability barriers; and (iv) formation of transmural pores in the inner membranes of E. coli is dependent upon the presence of C9 oligomers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of complement-dependent killing of Escherichia. coli.
the mechanism whereby the complement system mediates killing of serum-sensitive Escheriichia coli by the formation of transmural pores in the outer and inner membranes.
the mechanism of action of the terminal complement complexes on bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formation of transmural pores is a dynamic process, with the outer membrane being the primary site of attack and that the inner membrane is a secondary target.

C9 oligomer binding to C5b-91 complexes at 0 and/or 37 degrees C causes formation of pores in E. coli, but that the pores formed at low temperature are nonlethal, whereas those generated at 37 degrees cause loss of bacterial viability.
C9 binding to C5b-71C8 is not sufficient to kill E. coli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the C5b-6 complex, which is a potent bactericidal agent for serum-sensitive bacteria, does not kill these cells because it is unable to generate transmurally located pores in the outer membrane.
the complement system is capable of killing bacteria by two different mechanisms.

the C9 molecule, in addition to being the "catalytic subunit" of complement-mediated cytolysis, is also a "molecular switch" for triggering the formation of the transmural complement membrane attack complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complement system is a highly versatile effector mechanism, with the capacity to kill cells by multiple different means.
the complement pore is not a passive membrane lesion, but rather a dynamic structure that requires a complex series of interactions between the membrane and the complement proteins to form.

C9 binding to C5b-91C91 complexes is not a prerequisite for the generation of transmural pores in the E. coli outer and inner membranes, and that formation of such pores is a dynamic process that can occur in the absence of C9 binding.
